records.place: Colares, in the municipality of Sintra, Lisboa

wine.name: Arenae Ramisco
wine.grapes: Ramisco, the red grape of Colares, named on the label, from ungrafted vines rooted through the dune sand.
wine.sites: The members' plots in the dune sand between the Sintra hills and the Atlantic, the vines planted in trenches dug through the sand to the clay below, their trunks lying low on the sand behind stone walls and woven fences against the salt wind.
wine.making: Made at the co-operative's cellar from its members' grapes, the wine is fermented on its skins in stainless steel and aged for about five years, first in large vats of exotic wood and then in smaller oak casks in the vintages of 2012 to 2020 its merchants describe, before it is bottled in half litre bottles.
wine.glass: Dried rose, cedar and undergrowth with a breath of exotic spice, a hint of iodine and the salt air of the Atlantic; high, fresh acidity and marked, firm tannin keep it taut and long.
wine.ageing: Firm when released after its years in wood, it opens over a decade and more in bottle, and old Colares is known to last for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: Latin for sands: the co-operative's name for its Colares from the dunes.
The appellation under Sintra, demarcated in 1908, whose vines in the dune sand grow ungrafted.
The red grape of Colares, named on the label as the wine of the bottle.

records.table: Arenae Ramisco is the Colares red of the Adega Regional de Colares, the co-operative founded in 1931: Ramisco from ungrafted vines in the dune sand by the Atlantic, aged for years in wood. Expect dried rose, cedar and iodine on high acidity and firm tannin.
records.story: Colares was demarcated in 1908, a strip of dune sand between the Sintra hills and the Atlantic where vines are planted in trenches dug down to the clay, so deep in the sand that phylloxera cannot reach their roots. In 1931 the Adega Regional de Colares was founded, and from the start it vinified its members' grapes and vouched for the authenticity and quality of the wine; by its own account it is the oldest wine co-operative in Portugal. In the 1930s the law gave it the sole right to make Colares, so for some six decades every bottle of the appellation began in its cellar, whoever later aged and sold it. A decree of 15 September 1994 found that framework out of date and left the Adega to its work as a winemaking co-operative, and private houses could make Colares of their own again. By the end of the century the vineyard had shrunk to a small fraction of its size in the 1930s. Arenae, Latin for sands, is the name the Adega gives its Colares: Ramisco aged for years in wood before it is released. For a sommelier it is a plain way to pour a guest a wine of ungrafted European vines, from the cellar that kept the appellation alive.

others.name: Arenae Malvasia
others.note: The white of the same dunes, from Malvasia de Colares, under the same Arenae name.

traps: The Adega Regional de Colares was founded in 1931, but its sole right to make Colares came by law later in the 1930s and ended with a decree of 1994.
Colares is not the sand alone: its rules of 2021 also name the firmer chão rijo inland as a soil of the appellation, and let up to a fifth of a Colares come from vines there.

cards.front: Adega Regional de Colares: what does the name Arenae on its Colares mean?
cards.back: Sands, in Latin: the wine is Ramisco from ungrafted vines in the dune sand.

cards.front: What right did the law give the Adega Regional de Colares in the 1930s, and when did it end?
cards.back: The sole right to make Colares wine, for some six decades, until a decree of 15 September 1994 replaced that framework.

questions.q: A guest asks why the Ramisco vines behind Arenae grow on their own roots. Which reason fits?
opts: Phylloxera cannot reach roots deep in the dune sand
Grafting is forbidden on vineyards by the sea
Ramisco is too old a grape to take a rootstock
The vines are replanted from seed every few years
questions.exp: Phylloxera cannot travel through deep, loose dune sand to the roots, so vines planted through it to the clay below can stand ungrafted; no rule forbids grafting by the sea, and the sand, not the salt air, protects them.

questions.q: From the 1930s until a decree of 1994, every bottle of Colares began in one cellar. Whose was it?
opts: The Adega Regional de Colares
The Estação Agronómica Nacional
The house of Viúva Gomes
The palace cellar at Oeiras
questions.exp: The law gave the co-operative, founded in 1931, the sole right to make Colares until the decree of 1994; Viúva Gomes is a private house of Almoçageme, not the co-operative.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share of 35, one of them on arcolares.com, the Adega's own site; one fetch tried, of arcolares.com, refused because the host does not resolve here, so the site was read through search.

The Codex is in tension with the sources in js/data-questions.js: it says no grower could sell Colares without the Adega between 1931 and the 1990s, and that the Adega was founded in 1931 and held a legal monopoly for six decades; the founding is 1931, but the monopoly's legal basis is Decreto-Lei 24 500 of 19 September 1934 by the preamble of Decreto-Lei 235/94, and 1938 by Salt of Portugal and a GuildSomm article, so the record says the 1930s and some six decades.

Who founded the Adega is told three ways (the growers by GuildSomm, the farmers by a Norwegian paper, the government by Culinary Backstreets), so the record says only that it was founded in 1931; the collapse of the Brazilian market after 1929 as its cause rests on GuildSomm alone and is left out, and the claim of Portugal's oldest wine co-operative is told as the Adega's own.

Arenae's years in wood differ by source: sixty months in barrel (Decantalo, the 2016), at least six years in Brazilian mahogany (Aldeias Portuguesas), three years in vats of exotic wood and one in French oak (a writer's own wiki, not cited), so the making says about five years and names no vessel; fermentation in temperature controlled steel (Decantalo alone), Hedonism's 30 per cent whole bunches and a merchant's altitude of 110 metres are left out.

The glass draws on Decanter's note on the 2007 (dried roses, undergrowth, cedar, exotic spice, freshness), Hedonism's on the 2015 (a maritime character) and Garrafeira Nacional's on the 2010 (iodine, high acidity, marked tannin), all read through search; the half litre bottle rests on Decantalo and Garrafeira Nacional.

The shrinking of the vineyard rests on two accounts read through search (over a thousand hectares in the 1930s, twelve or so in the late 1990s), one of them a critic's own site, which is not cited, so no figure is given; Chão Rijo, the Adega's regional wine from the clay, rests on one source and is left out of others.

Living names met and kept out of the record: the Adega's oenologist, quoted in a critic's report, and the writer of the GuildSomm article, whose name is in its address, which is why that article is not listed.

records.place: Almoçageme, Colares, in the municipality of Sintra, Lisboa

wine.name: Viúva Gomes Colares Tinto
wine.grapes: Ramisco, from ungrafted vines in the sand.
wine.sites: Ungrafted vines in the dune sand around Almoçageme, between the Sintra hills and the Atlantic: the house's own small plots, with grapes bought from local growers in chosen vineyards.
wine.making: Whole bunches are fermented in tank and trodden by foot, with long skin contact; the wine is then aged for five years and more, by vintage, in casks of French oak, Portuguese chestnut and Brazilian mahogany before release.
wine.glass: Light and precise, with wild berries and damp earth over bright, high acidity and firm tannin; old bottles turn to leather and forest floor and keep their grip.
wine.ageing: Taut and firm when released after its years in cask, it lasts for decades: the house has released bottles of the 1960s that are firm and alive.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant an old bottle gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The old spelling of Colares, the same appellation, which the house keeps on its red.
Portuguese for the widow Gomes, the name the house has traded under.
Red: the Ramisco wine, made beside a white of Malvasia de Colares.

records.table: Viúva Gomes is a Colares house of Almoçageme dating from 1808 by its own account, and its Colares Tinto is Ramisco from ungrafted vines in the sand, trodden by foot and aged for years in cask. Light, firm and fresh, it lasts for decades.
records.story: In 1808, as the house tells it, a cellar was built in the village of Almoçageme, under the Sintra hills, to make the wine of Colares, and the name the house has traded under means the widow Gomes. A century later, in 1908, Colares was demarcated: a strip of dune sand by the Atlantic where vines are planted down to the clay, out of phylloxera's reach. In 1931 the Adega Regional de Colares was founded to vinify the growers' grapes and vouch for the wine, and in the 1930s the law gave the co-operative the sole right to make Colares, so for some six decades the wine of every house, Viúva Gomes among them, began in its cellar. A decree of 1994 ended that framework, and the house makes its own Colares again, from its small plots and the vineyards of local growers: whole bunches trodden by foot, then aged for five years and more in casks of oak, chestnut and Brazilian mahogany. Its label keeps the old spelling, Collares. From its cellar the house has also released old vintages of the 1960s, and they show what Ramisco from the sand becomes with time: firm and alive after half a century. For a sommelier, it is the Colares to open when a guest asks what an old ungrafted European vine tastes like.

others.name: Viúva Gomes Colares Branco
others.note: The white of Malvasia de Colares from the same sand, made beside the red.

others.name: Viúva Gomes Viticultores
others.note: A Vinho Regional Lisboa red and white from vines inside the Colares area but off the sand, so outside the appellation's rules, by the house's account.

traps: Collares on a Viúva Gomes label is the old spelling of Colares, the same appellation, not another place.
Viúva Gomes is a private house in Almoçageme, not the Adega Regional de Colares, the co-operative of the same appellation.

cards.front: Viúva Gomes: how is its Colares Tinto made before release?
cards.back: Ramisco fermented as whole bunches and trodden by foot, then aged five years and more in casks of oak, chestnut and mahogany.

cards.front: Which spelling of the appellation does the Viúva Gomes red print on its label?
cards.back: Collares, the old spelling with a double l, for the appellation Colares.

questions.q: A guest notices Collares, spelt with a double l, on a bottle of Viúva Gomes red. What does it mean?
opts: The old spelling of the Colares appellation
A wine from the clay outside the appellation
A reserve bottling aged longer in cask
A wine from grafted vines of the estate
questions.exp: Collares is the old spelling that Viúva Gomes keeps for the appellation Colares itself; it marks no other place, no reserve and no wine from outside the appellation.

questions.q: Viúva Gomes dates its cellar in Almoçageme to the year of its founding. Which year does the house give?
questions.exp: The house dates itself to 1808, a century before Colares was demarcated in 1908; 1931 is the year the Adega Regional de Colares was founded.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35, two of them on viuvagomes.com and the rest outside it; no fetch tried.

1808 is the house's own date (its history page, Winetourism, Salt of Portugal), so the story hedges it; the founder is named José Gomes da Silva in two accounts but his dates are in none, so he is not named.

Salt of Portugal alone tells that the founder's widow and sons carried the business on, that the house changed hands in 1920 and 1931 and that it was bought in 1988 with its vineyards, its cellar and old vintages back to the early twentieth century; with no second source the story says only that the name means the widow Gomes.

The father and son who keep the house are living and are not named (José and Diogo Baeta in the sources, for people.json); the house's manifesto calls them its fourth and fifth generations of guardians, which is left out as a present role.

The making rests on Leon and Son (whole bunches trodden by foot, own yeasts in steel, long skin contact, about five years in French oak, chestnut and mahogany) and Union Square Wines (whole clusters, five years before release); Shrine to the Vine gives nearly a decade in French oak and Brazilian mahogany, so the record says five years and more.

The spelling Collares on the red rests on Decanter, Union Square Wines and Shrine to the Vine; the old vintages of the 1960s on Shrine to the Vine (1969), Dagens Naeringsliv (1965, 1967) and Garrafeira Nacional (1965); the glass on Leon and Son (light, precise, high tannin and acidity), Cask Cartel's note on the 2014 (berries, earth, firm tannin, bright acidity) and Dagens Naeringsliv (leather).
Organic farming is claimed by one importer (Keeling Andrew) and denied by Winetourism, so nothing is said of it; the house's few hectares and its bottles a year are volatile and left out.

wine.name: Prova Régia Arinto
wine.appellation: Bucelas, or Vinho Regional Lisboa in some vintages
wine.grapes: Arinto alone, the grape of Bucelas, known in the Minho as Pedernã.
wine.sites: Bucelas, a short way north of Lisbon, where the estate's own vineyards are planted mostly to Arinto.
wine.making: Pressed and fermented cool in stainless steel, at 13 to 18 degrees Celsius by vintage on the sheets of the house and its merchants; the wine then rests three to six months on its fine lees, stirred, with no oak at all.
wine.glass: Lemon, lime and green apple skin with a touch of jasmine and orange blossom and a saline, oyster shell finish; crisp and taut, with keen acidity and a light texture rounded by the lees.
wine.ageing: A light, fresh white made to be drunk young, while its lemon and green apple are bright and its acidity keen.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanter; a white wine glass.

label.means: Royal approval: the name recalls the Bucelas wine taken to the English court.
The white only appellation north of Lisbon, demarcated in 1911, built on Arinto; some vintages carry Vinho Regional Lisboa instead.
The grape, named on the label because the wine is made from it alone.

records.table: Prova Régia is the white of Quinta da Romeira at Bucelas, north of Lisbon: Arinto alone, fermented cool in steel and never put in oak. Expect lemon, green apple and a saline finish on keen acidity: a white for grilled fish and shellfish.
records.story: Quinta da Romeira lies at Bucelas, just north of Lisbon; its owners trace its documents to 1218, and the morgado of Santa Catherina, the entailed estate it belonged to, to 1703. During the Peninsular War, as the story is told, the Duke of Wellington (1769 to 1852) came to know the white wine of Bucelas and took it home to England for the king, and the name Prova Régia, royal approval, recalls that story. In 1911 Bucelas was demarcated as an appellation of white wine alone, with Arinto at its heart. Prova Régia, Arinto fermented in steel and kept away from oak, became the label by which British merchants knew the estate. Sogrape's purchase of Quinta da Romeira, its first foothold in the Lisboa region, was made public at the start of 2019, and the group later took back the old spelling of the name, Romeyra, for the brand, which it presents as a new chapter for the Arinto of Bucelas. For a sommelier, Prova Régia is the plain lesson of Bucelas: a dry, saline white of one grape from the edge of the capital, to pour with the fish course.

others.name: Morgado de Santa Catherina
others.note: The estate's second Bucelas Arinto label, made beside Prova Régia.

others.name: Prova Régia Reserva
others.note: A Reserva white of Arinto alone under the same name.

traps: Quinta da Romeira and Quinta da Romeyra are one estate in Bucelas, the second the old spelling its owners took back, not two houses.
Bucelas is an appellation for white wine alone; Prova Régia is a dry white of Arinto, never a red or a fortified wine.
Prova Régia has been sold as DOC Bucelas in some vintages and as Vinho Regional Lisboa in others, so read the label before calling a bottle Bucelas.

cards.front: Prova Régia: what does the name mean, and what story does it recall?
cards.back: Royal approval: in the time of the Peninsular War the Duke of Wellington is said to have taken Bucelas wine home to the king.

cards.front: Which grape makes Quinta da Romeira Prova Régia, and in what is it fermented?
cards.back: Arinto alone, fermented cool in stainless steel, with no oak.

questions.q: A guest who wants an oak aged white asks about Quinta da Romeira Prova Régia. What should you tell them?
opts: It is fermented in steel and sees no oak
It is fermented and aged in new French oak
It spends a year in large old chestnut casks
It is aged under a veil of flor yeast
questions.exp: Prova Régia is Arinto fermented cool in stainless steel and rested on its fine lees, with no oak at all; new French oak would give vanilla and toast that it does not have.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35, on sogrape.com, importers' and merchants' domains and Infovini, and one shared with Villa Oeiras for the dates of Wellington and Pombal (Britannica and Wikipedia, read through search, which are the sources for 1769 to 1852); no fetch tried.

Sogrape's purchase is dated to the start of 2019 by Agroportal (4 January 2019), Wine Spectator (February 2019, the deal closed the month before) and The Drinks Business (February 2019); Liberty Wines gives 2018, which the record does not follow.
founded is empty: Sogrape traces the estate's documents to 1218 and Liberty Wines and other merchants date its wine to 1703, so the story tells both as accounts.

Wellington's gift goes to George III in Infovini and one Liberty page and to George IV in another, so the record says the king; his staying at the estate and a restoration from 1988 rest on one account each and are left out.

The making rests on Liberty Wines' sheet for the 2020 (short skin contact, pneumatic press, steel at 16 to 18 degrees, six months on the fine lees with stirring) and The Wine Society's for the 2024 (no oak); Liberty also says the vintages before 2019 drew Arinto from across the Lisboa region, which the record leaves out for want of a second source and because it sits oddly with a Bucelas label.

The plan's why, that Prova Régia made Arinto known abroad, is softened to the label British merchants knew the estate by; the plan's one listing of Sogrape as maker is confirmed as ownership from 2019; the claim of Portugal's largest Arinto vineyard (Wine Spectator, Agroportal) is left out as a size.

The seller, named as a family in Wine Spectator, is not named; Sogrape's living chief executive and the estate's living winemaker appear in the sources and nowhere in the record; Espumante Bruto in others rests on the importer's list alone.

records.place: Oeiras, on the coast west of Lisbon, Carcavelos, Lisboa

wine.name: Villa Oeiras Carcavelos Superior 15 Anos
wine.grapes: Arinto, Galego Dourado and Ratinho, the white grapes of Carcavelos.
wine.sites: The vineyards on the old estate of the Marquis of Pombal at Oeiras, near the mouth of the Tagus, replanted in the 1980s, with the plantings the council added later.
wine.making: The fermentation is stopped midway with grape spirit from Lourinhã, by the house's account, and the wine is aged in Portuguese and French oak barrels, fifteen years on average across the blend; the appellation asks at least two years in wood and six months in bottle.
wine.glass: Golden amber, with dried apricot, bitter orange, toasted hazelnut and toffee over a note of tobacco; rich and medium sweet, with a saline lift of sea air, fresh acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink, its long ageing done in the house's casks rather than in bottle, so it needs no cellaring before it is poured.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, lightly chilled; it needs no decanter; a small white wine glass and a modest measure.

label.means: The appellation of fortified wine on the coast west of Lisbon, demarcated in 1908.
As the house gives it, more than ten years in wood and the approval of the regional tasting panel.
Fifteen years: the average time in oak of the wines in the blend.
The brand of the Oeiras municipal council's Carcavelos project.

records.table: Villa Oeiras is the Carcavelos of the Oeiras council, grown on an old estate on the coast west of Lisbon. Its Superior 15 Anos is fortified Arinto, Galego Dourado and Ratinho aged for years in oak: dried apricot, bitter orange and hazelnut, medium sweet and saline.
records.story: Carcavelos is the fortified wine of the coast west of Lisbon, and the Marquis of Pombal (1699 to 1782), the minister who rebuilt Lisbon after the earthquake of 1755, made it on his family estate at Oeiras, from 1752 by the council's account. The appellation was demarcated in 1908, but oidium, mildew and phylloxera had already struck its vines, and through the twentieth century the villas, hotels and suburbs of the growing city covered its vineyards, until only two producers were left. In the 1980s, from 1983 by the council's account, the national agronomy station, the Estação Agronómica Nacional, replanted vines on the Marquis's old estate, and the Oeiras council later joined it in a partnership to save the wine. The council created the brand Villa Oeiras, equipped a cellar at Casal da Manteiga, in use from 2001, extended the vineyard and, by its own account, recovered the palace's old wine cellar in 2012. Its Carcavelos is made in the modern way, the fermentation stopped with grape spirit, where, by the house's account, the nineteenth century had fermented the wine dry and fortified it with vinho abafado, and it is aged for years in Portuguese and French oak. To a sommelier, Villa Oeiras is the revival of Carcavelos in a glass: a fortified wine of white grapes, aged in wood, from an appellation the city almost erased.

others.name: Villa Oeiras Carcavelos 7 Anos
others.note: The younger blend, aged seven years on average in Portuguese and French oak, by the house's own page.

traps: Carcavelos is a fortified wine of white grapes from the coast west of Lisbon, not a Port and not a Moscatel de Setúbal.
Superior on a Villa Oeiras label means more than ten years in wood with the tasting panel's approval, as the house explains it, not a sweeter or stronger wine.

cards.front: Villa Oeiras: on whose old estate at Oeiras are its Carcavelos vines grown?
cards.back: The Marquis of Pombal's, replanted in the 1980s by the national agronomy station and later farmed with the Oeiras council.

cards.front: What do Superior and 15 Anos mean on a bottle of Villa Oeiras Carcavelos?
cards.back: More than ten years in wood with the regional tasting panel's approval, and an average age in oak of fifteen years.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35, three of them on oeiras.pt, villaoeiras.com and the IVV, and one shared with Quinta da Romeira for the dates of Pombal and Wellington; no fetch tried.

founded is empty: the council's pages give a protocol with the agronomy station in 1988 and in 1997, other accounts give 1986 and 2006 for the partnership and 2001 and 2009 for the first commercial wine or the brand, so the story says only that the council later joined the replanting of 1983, which the council and Euronews both date.

The Marquis of Pombal's dates, 1699 to 1782, rest on Britannica and Wikipedia read through search, as the plan's note allowed; his wine from 1752 is the council's own account, and another council page dates the first records of Carcavelos wine to the fifteenth century.

The decline (oidium, mildew and phylloxera, then villas, hotels and suburbs, two producers left by 1983) rests on Euronews and Decanter's Carcavelos feature; Villa Oeiras as the sole producer (Haus Alpenz, Euronews) is left out as a present claim, since Haus Alpenz also lists Quinta dos Pesos Carcavelos of 1989 and 1998, and the plan's almost the only maker is not repeated.

The fortification midway with spirit from Lourinhã and the meaning of Superior are the house's own pages; the minimum of two years in wood and six months in bottle is the IVV's specification for the DOP, which allows both mutage and a dry wine fortified with vinho abafado; the nineteenth century's dry fermentation is the house's history.

The glass draws on the house's notes (golden amber, dried fruit and nuts, spices, tobacco, toffee, medium sweet, rich, long), Haus Alpenz (dried apricot, bitter orange, toasted hazelnut, sea air) and Decanter (dried apricot, honey, caramelised orange); Haus Alpenz's calcareous soils near the Tagus and its vines from Pombal's own cuttings rest on it alone and are left out.

The house's Superior page and its 15 Anos page are read as one wine, as Garrafeira Nacional and Decanter list it (Superior 15 anos); if the house sells them as two, the checker should part them. The serve follows the Codex's line for tawny wines; the only figure read, 8 to 10 degrees, is a merchant's for the 7 Anos.

records.place: Alenquer, in the hills north of Lisbon, Lisboa

wine.name: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro Reserva
wine.grapes: Syrah from several plots, with a few per cent of Viognier fermented together with it.
wine.sites: Plots of Syrah on the rolling slopes behind the winery near Alenquer, on clay and limestone that vary from parcel to parcel, some twenty kilometres from the Atlantic in a steady wind, farmed organically.
wine.making: Picked by hand, destemmed without crushing and fermented with the Viognier in temperature controlled stainless steel vats, with a long maceration; the wine is then aged for sixteen to twenty months, by vintage, in French oak barrels, about two fifths of them new.
wine.glass: Violet, damson and blackberry with black pepper, a little cherry and a touch of dark chocolate, the oak held in the background; full but supple, with velvety tannin, fresh acidity and a long, firm finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable after a few years in bottle, it lasts a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The regional wine of Lisboa: the Reserva is not labelled with the Alenquer appellation, though its vines grow there.
The house's Syrah with a little Viognier, made above its plain red.
The estate near Alenquer whose own organically farmed vineyards give the wine.

records.table: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro Reserva is Syrah from the hills of Alenquer north of Lisbon, fermented with a little Viognier in the manner of Côte-Rôtie and aged in French oak. Violet, damson and black pepper on velvety tannin: pour it as you would a northern Rhône red.
records.story: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro lies near Alenquer, in the hills north of Lisbon, some twenty kilometres from the Atlantic and open to its steady wind. By most accounts in 1990, the estate was bought by a gastronome with a passion for the wines of the Rhône, who planted it mostly with Syrah, from cuttings brought from the Rhône, and with Viognier, the grapes of the northern Rhône. The new estate made its opening wine with the 1997 vintage. The Reserva, Syrah from several plots fermented with a few per cent of Viognier as Côte-Rôtie does, and aged in French oak, became the estate's flagship, the wine with which it set out to show what Syrah can do in the Atlantic hills of Lisboa. From the 2006 harvest the estate began its conversion to organic farming, with new labels for a new phase of its history, and its vineyards were later certified organic. The Reserva is labelled Vinho Regional Lisboa rather than DOC Alenquer. For a sommelier, it is the Portuguese Syrah to pour beside a northern Rhône red: perfumed, peppery and supple, from vines a short drive from the capital.

traps: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro Reserva is labelled Vinho Regional Lisboa, not DOC Alenquer, though the estate lies in Alenquer.
The Viognier in the Reserva is fermented with the Syrah, a few per cent of the whole, not a white wine blended in afterwards.

cards.front: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro Reserva: what is in the bottle, and how is the Viognier used?
cards.back: Syrah from several plots with a few per cent of Viognier, fermented together, as in Côte-Rôtie.

cards.front: With which vintage did Quinta do Monte d'Oiro make its first wine, and when did its organic conversion begin?
cards.back: The first wine came with the 1997 vintage; the conversion to organic farming began with the 2006 harvest.

questions.exp: The Reserva is Syrah from several plots fermented with a few per cent of Viognier, in the manner of the northern Rhône; Syrah blended with Touriga Nacional is a Portuguese pairing, not this wine.

questions.q: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro began to convert its vineyards to organic farming. With which harvest did it begin?
questions.exp: The conversion began with the 2006 harvest, nine years after the estate's opening wine of 1997; 1997 is that wine's vintage, not the year of the conversion.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35, one of them on quintadomontedoiro.com, which returned only its home page; no fetch tried.

founded is empty, as the plan's note asked: the purchase is 1987 in one account and the 1980s in another, and the estate's past is taken to the seventeenth century in marketing copy and its buildings to the early nineteenth century in another, so the story says the late 1980s; the first wine of 1997 rests on several accounts.

The man who bought and planted the estate is living and is never named (José Bento dos Santos in the sources, for people.json), nor the winemaker and consultant named on the importer's sheet; the joint wine with the Rhône house of Chapoutier, Ex Aequo, rests on a writer's own site and one other mention and is left out.

The appellation is Vinho Regional Lisboa on the importer's technical sheet (Alt Wines), and Wine-Searcher lists the Reserva as Regional Lisbon, though one merchant files it under Alenquer; the checker should confirm the label.

The making rests on the Alt Wines sheet (picked by hand, destemmed uncrushed, steel, long maceration, 16 to 18 months, 40 per cent new), Amathus (18 to 20 months, 40 per cent new) and a profile of the 2013 (16 to 20 months), so the record gives sixteen to twenty months by vintage.

The organic conversion from the 2006 harvest rests on two accounts and the certification on the Alt Wines sheet; the sites (rolling slopes behind the winery, some twenty kilometres from the ocean in a steady wind, clay and limestone varying by parcel) on Wines of Portugal and Wine Trail Traveler.

The plan's why, that the estate proved Syrah belongs in Lisboa, is softened to an aim; the first vintage of Parcela 24 (2007) and its northern Rhône cuttings rest on one account and are left out, and Madrigal's Viognier rests on its name and one listing.

The glass draws on Amathus (violets, damson, perfumed fruit), Garrafeira Tio Pepe and Vinalda (black pepper, discreet oak), Wine and Stuff on the 2011 (blackberry, cherry, chocolate) and two merchants on velvety tannin and a long, firm finish.
